label: rem:square-series-multisummability-prior-art
title: Prior art: the square of a single-slope $q$-series needs two levels of summation
html:
Di Vizio, Ramis, Sauloy and Zhang work through the series \hat y = \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n(n-1)/2} x^n, whose equation has a single non-trivial slope, and its square \hat Y = \hat y^{\,2} [divizio-ramis-sauloy-zhang, \S 4.4, p. 43]. The q-Borel transform of \hat Y is meromorphic on \mathbb{C} with simple poles in q^{\mathbb{N}} and has q-exponential growth of order exactly two at infinity, so \hat Y is not q-Borel–Laplace summable at a single level as \hat y is. The equation of \hat Y,

\Delta \hat Y = 1 + x, \qquad \Delta = q^2 x^3 \sigma_q^2 - x(1+x)\sigma_q + 1 = (x\sigma_q - 1)(x^2\sigma_q - 1),

has two non-trivial slopes, and \hat Y is (1, \tfrac12)-summable by a composite procedure: a q-Borel transform, an acceleration, then a q-Laplace transform of level \tfrac12 [divizio-ramis-sauloy-zhang, Remark 4.12, eq. (4.12.1), Theorem 4.13, p. 44].

What this gives here. The module \mathcal{K} of the conjecture is pure isoclinic of slope \tfrac12 at x = \infty. Products and squares of its solutions are governed by \mathcal{K}^{\otimes 2}, which the bar-parity conjecture records as anisoclinic with slopes \{+1, 0, -1\}. The worked example shows, for one explicit series, the same phenomenon: squaring a single-slope series produces an equation with more than one slope, and its formal solutions then need a multi-level summation. A summation argument for the squares f_\pm^{2} therefore cannot be inherited from one for f_\pm; it has to be made at the levels of \mathcal{K}^{\otimes 2}.

What it does not supply. The example concerns one series with integral slopes and is not a theorem about \mathcal{K}. It does not settle whether the formal solution of \mathcal{K} at infinity, whose slope \tfrac12 is not integral, is summable at a single level after the ramification q \mapsto q^{1/2}, or only by a multi-level procedure. The test that Remark 4.12 applies would discriminate the two readings: compute the q-Borel transform of that formal solution and find the order of its q-exponential growth at infinity. Nor does the example show that the levels of \hat Y match those of \mathcal{K}^{\otimes 2}.
